items.stem: “Pariksha Guru is considered landmark in the history of Hindi novel.” Justify the statement with suitable arguments.
items.answer: Pariksha Guru, the first Hindi novel, tells the story of the extravagance of Hindu bankers and traders, and its theme is that modern life should be embraced without abandoning Indian culture. (1) It cautioned young men of well-to-do families about the ill effects of bad company. (2) It showed how to live a practical life that preserves traditional values in honour and dignity. (3) It advised children to read the newspaper. (4) The author emphasised that modernity should be embraced without giving up middle class values. (5) The novel tries to teach the reader the ‘right way’ to live, expecting ‘sensible men’ to be worldly-wise and practical, rooted in the values of their own tradition and culture, and to live with dignity and honour. (6) Its characters attempt to bridge two different worlds: they take to new agricultural technology, modernise trading practices and change the use of Indian languages so that they can carry both Western science and Indian wisdom. Because no earlier novel had attempted this, Pariksha Guru is rightly called a landmark in the history of the Hindi novel.

items.stem: Distinguish between the themes of ‘Pride and Prejudice’ and ‘Jane Eyre’ novels written by Jane Austen and Charlotte Bronte respectively.
items.answer: For both novelists the main idea of the novel centres on women, but the two writers hold different ideas and opinions. (1) The first line of Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice states that “It is a universally acknowledged truth, that a single man in possession of good fortune, must be in want of a wife”; Austen’s observation shows that women of that society were always preoccupied with the perception of marriage and money. Her novels give a glimpse of the world of women in genteel rural society in early-nineteenth-century Britain and make us think about a society that encouraged women to look for ‘good’ marriages and wealthy or propertied husbands, so her main characters typify that society. (2) In Charlotte Bronte’s Jane Eyre, young Jane is shown as independent and assertive at a time when girls were expected to be quiet and well behaved; at the age of ten she protests against the hypocrisy of her elders with startling bluntness. Bronte dealt with women who broke the established norms of society before adjusting to them, and such stories allowed women readers to sympathise with rebellious actions. Thus Austen mirrors the marriage-and-money world of genteel women, while Bronte projects the rebellious, self-assertive woman.
items.ocr: The book prints the publication year of Jane Eyre as 1874; the novel was in fact published in 1847. The stem itself is unaffected.

items.stem: Explain the impact of print culture on the religious reforms in India during nineteenth century.
items.answer: (1) Print led to intense controversies between social and religious reformers and Hindu orthodoxy over matters like widow immolation, monotheism, the Brahmanical priestly system and idolatry. (2) With the coming of print, ulama feared that colonial rulers would encourage conversion; to counter this they used cheap lithographic presses, published Persian and Urdu translations of holy scriptures and printed religious newspapers and tracts. (3) Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821 and Hindu orthodoxy commissioned the Samachar Chandrika to oppose his opinions. (4) In Bengal, as the debate developed, tracts and newspapers proliferated and circulated a variety of arguments. (5) A number of Muslim sects and seminaries appeared, each with a different interpretation of faith, each keen on enlarging its following and countering the influence of its opponents. Print therefore turned religious reform into a public, argumentative movement that reached far beyond the elite.
items.ocr: Point (2) of the printed answer reads ‘mamas feared’, a misprint for ‘ulama feared’; corrected in the solution.

items.stem:
“Oral culture and print culture were complimentary to each other.” Justify the statement with any three suitable arguments.
or
How did print bring the reading public and hearing public closer ? Explain.
or
Highlight any three circumstances that led to the intermingling of the hearing culture and the reading culture.
items.answer: (1) Earlier, reading was restricted to the elites. (2) With the printing press books could reach wider sections of society; if earlier there was only a hearing public, now a reading public came into being. (3) Publishers had to keep in mind the wider reach of printed books, because even those who could not read could enjoy listening to books being read out. (4) So printers began publishing popular ballads and folk tales, and such books were profusely illustrated with pictures. (5) These were then sung and recited at gatherings in villages and in taverns in towns, so the line that separated the oral and reading cultures became blurred. (6) In this way the hearing public and the reading public became intermingled, and the two cultures supported each other.

items.stem: Describe any five strategies developed by the printers and publishers in the 19th century to sell their products.
items.answer: In the nineteenth century printers and publishers continuously developed new strategies to sell their products. (1) Periodicals serialised famous novels, which gave birth to a particular way of writing novels; in 1863 Charles Dickens’s ‘Pickwick Papers’ was serialised in a magazine, and magazines were attractive to readers because they were illustrated and cheap, so readers bought them eagerly. (2) In 1920s England popular works were sold in cheap series called the Shilling Series. (3) The dust cover or book jacket was introduced to make the book more attractive to readers. (4) Books were printed on the offset press, which could print in six colours at a time. (5) To sustain buying during the Great Depression of the 1930s, publishers brought out cheap paperback editions, which soon became a big hit. These devices kept books affordable and desirable and widened the market for print.

items.stem: How did the invention of Printing Press help the emergence of Renaissance ?
items.answer: The printing press increased the number of books, newspapers, magazines, pamphlets and other reading material, and with more of these things more people gained easy access to knowledge. The new knowledge increased rational thinking and helped greatly in reducing superstition and orthodoxy in religion as well as in society. Very soon the new atmosphere began to appear in the political life of several countries of Europe and other parts of the world. It was a Renaissance in terms of material progress although premature in terms of enlightenment; its consequences were apparent in the use and misuse of new skills, expertise, efficiency and authority. Creative and destructive powers alike found support in the technological change brought by print. Human minds of every temperament — genteel, aggressive or dull — took help from print technology. The Renaissance was thus seen in technological change, mechanical development and the industrial age, even as it left society divided into two classes, capitalists and proletariats.

items.stem: How did print culture affect women in the nineteenth century India ? Explain
items.answer: The number of women readers swelled enormously in middle class homes, for the following reasons. (1) Many magazines and books were written mainly for women and published. (2) Print culture gave women some amount of freedom to read and to develop their own views on various issues, especially those concerning women. (3) Issues such as women’s education, widowhood and widow re-marriage came to be liberally debated in print. (4) Women novelists such as Jane Austen and the Bronte sisters in Europe and Kailashbasini Debi and Pandita Ramabai in India represented a new type of woman — a woman with the power to think and the ability to act with determination. (5) Girls, especially from the middle classes, began to enrol in school in large numbers. In a word, print culture heralded the arrival of a new woman.

items.stem: Describe the progress of print in Japan.
items.answer: (1) Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing technology into Japan around 768–770 C.E. The oldest Japanese book, printed in 868 C.E., is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, containing six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations; pictures were also printed on textiles, playing cards and paper money. (2) In medieval Japan poets and prose writers were regularly published, and books were cheap and abundant. (3) Printing of visual material led to interesting publishing practices: in the late eighteenth century, in the flourishing urban circles at Edo (later to be known as Tokyo), illustrated collections of paintings depicted an elegant urban culture involving artists, courtesans and teahouse gatherings. (4) Libraries and bookstores were packed with hand-printed material of various types — books on women, musical instruments, calculations, the tea ceremony, flower arrangements, proper etiquette, cooking and famous places. Print thus grew from a religious craft into the basis of a wide popular urban culture in Japan.

items.stem:
Discuss the position of printing technology in 17th century China. How was it affected by western technology in 19th century ?
or
How did the uses of print technology develop in China by the 17th century ? Explain.
items.answer: Development of printing technology in seventeenth century China: (1) By the seventeenth century, as urban culture bloomed in China, the uses of print diversified. Print was no longer used just by scholars and officials; merchants also used print in their everyday life as they collected trade information. (2) Reading increasingly became a leisure activity, and the new readership preferred fictional narratives, poetry, autobiographies, anthologies of literary masterpieces and romantic plays. (3) Rich women began to read, and many women began publishing their poetry and plays; wives of scholar-officials published their works and courtesans wrote about their lives. Effect of western technology in nineteenth century China: (1) Since hand printing had started in China, books began reaching a public that included children, both boys and girls, youths, adults and senior people, and all shared in the exchange of scientific, theological and practical thought; bureaucrats now came through examinations such as the civil service examinations held there. (2) School textbooks on the western education system came in a glut, which many felt polluted Chinese culture, though they also accommodated socialisation once the Western powers established their roots in China.

items.stem:
How did the print material of Europe affected the rise of nationalism in India ?
or
How did print culture contribute to growth of nationalism in India ?
items.answer: (1) Western education had been widening the horizon of understanding of a number of things among Indians. (2) It gave educated Indians a rational, secular, democratic and national outlook; western thinkers like Rousseau, Paine and John Stuart Mill greatly influenced the Indian intelligentsia. (3) Italian nationalists like Garibaldi, Mazzini and Cavour also greatly influenced them. (4) When educated Indians came in contact with western education it opened their eyes. (5) Translation of western literature into Indian languages proved highly useful in bringing about a new awakening both in the cities and in the villages. (6) Revolutions like the American War of Independence and the French Revolution gave the thoughts of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity to the whole world. (7) The spirit of nationalism and patriotism made Indians forget their differences and inspired them to smash the wheels of oppression and exploitation that had been crushing their very existence for several centuries.

items.stem: What were the important features of European literature ? How did it help in spreading new or progressive ideas in the continent ?
items.answer: The important features of European literature were as follows. (1) The new literary works of different European authors, poets and languages helped greatly in promoting new and progressive ideas; this literature was concerned with social injustice and with nationalism. (2) The writers of modern Europe tried their best to promote realism and to avoid meagre idealism; realism was reflected very well in the works of Charles Dickens and Thomas Hardy in England, Leo Tolstoy, Ivan Turgenev and Dostoevsky in Russia, and Balzac, Flaubert, Emile Zola and Anatole France in France. (3) Human suffering during World War I increased enormously; these events of pathos stirred sensitive people, who put their feelings on paper (palm leaves or handmade), and such people were known as playwrights, dramatists, poets, philosophers, scientists and researchers. (4) Renowned authors like James Joyce (Ireland), Marcel Proust (France), Virginia Woolf (England) and Scott Fitzgerald (USA) made their fortune and glory with the help of advanced printing technology. (5) The exuberance and overflow of cheap books like chapbooks and the Bibliotheque Bleue gave pain to scholars such as Erasmus, who felt such books deceived the eye and pumped ignorance into the minds of adolescents all over Europe. (6) European literature also covered the countryside (folk tales, songs, stories, fables), schooling, training, course books, books on entertainment, and books on science and theology such as Gutenberg’s Bible. Together these writings carried new and progressive ideas across the continent.

items.stem: How did the printing and writing of Indian History during the late 19th and early 20th centuries prove a mixed blessing for the Indian society ?
items.answer: (a) Indians lost confidence in their own capacity for self-government. Many British officials and writers of the time constantly advanced the thesis that Indians had never been able to rule themselves in the past, that the Hindus and Muslims had always fought each other, that Indians were destined to be ruled by foreigners, and that their religion and social life were degraded and uncivilised, making them unfit for democracy or even self-government. (b) Many nationalist leaders pointed to the cultural heritage of India with pride and referred the critics to the political achievements of rulers like Ashoka and Chandragupta Vikramaditya; some nationalists went to the extreme of glorifying India’s past uncritically, ignoring its weaknesses and backwardness. (c) Great harm was done, in particular, by the tendency to look up only to the heritage of ancient India while ignoring the equally great achievements of the medieval period. (d) This encouraged the growth of communal sentiments among the Muslims, who began looking to the history of the Arabs and the Turks for cultural and historical inspiration while their feet were living in Indian land. Printed history therefore both awakened national pride and sowed communal division — a mixed blessing.

items.stem: Describe main aims and suggestions of the Press Commission of 1952 C.E.
items.answer: The Government of India appointed a Press Commission in 1952. It consisted of 11 members and its Chairman was Justice G. S. Rajadhyaksha; it submitted its report in 1954. Its aims were: (1) to safeguard the freedom of the Press; (2) to censure objectionable types of journalistic conduct; (3) to encourage a sense of responsibility and public service among journalists; (4) to keep under review developments likely to restrict the supply and fair distribution of news of public interest and importance; (5) to improve methods of recruitment and training for the journalistic profession; and (6) to study developments in the Press and suggest measures to check the concentration of the Press in a few hands. Suggestions: the Commission suggested banning cross-word puzzle competitions in newspapers and periodicals, and recommended that not more than 40% of the total space should be covered by advertisements; this put teeth into the income side of printing and kept printers submissive. Conclusion: most of the suggestions of this Commission were accepted by the Government of India and incorporated in law.
items.ocr: The stem is printed as ‘Press Commission of 1C.E.’; the answer shows this is the Press Commission of 1952 C.E., so the year is restored in the stem.

items.stem: The books are considered an effective means of spreading progress and enlightenment. Justify the statement how ?
items.answer: (1) All the great revolutions — the Protestant Reformation, the Union of England and Scotland in 1707, the Declaration of American Independence and the like — took place when print culture spread in Europe and the Americas, because books made people able to understand the importance of freedom. (2) Playwrights, poets and authors like Shakespeare, Mathew Arnold, Abul Fazal, Ayodhya Singh Upadhyay, Mulk Raj Anand, William Blake, Bhartrihari and Bankim Chandra Chatterjee were products of that period. (3) Cartoons, caricatures and several types of painting indicate the sensitivity of human minds and bring out even the most concealed human emotions. (4) So far as enlightenment is concerned, it remained confined to philosophers, anthropologists and philanthropists, because the viruses of domination, imperialism and ego stood in the way of understanding the European West. Books therefore carried progress and enlightenment to whole societies, even if the deepest enlightenment reached only a few.

items.stem: Discuss briefly the growth of modern press in 19th century in India.
items.answer: The growth of the modern press in nineteenth century India was as follows. (1) The growth of the press started with the arrival of print culture in India and happened in the later years of the nineteenth century. (2) Prior to the arrival of print culture in India, palm leaves or handmade paper were used for writing and copying manuscripts, and such books were bound with wooden sheets. (3) The first print in India was the Bengal Gazette, a weekly magazine edited by James Augustus Hickey; thereafter its Bangla edition was also published by some Bengali scholars under the guidance of Raja Ram Mohan Roy. (4) Other newspapers followed this trend — Amrit Bazar Patrika, Yugantar (Bengali) and Kesari (Marathi); watchwords like Vande Mataram became a jewel in every mouth during India’s freedom struggle. (5) Sambad Kaumudi (1821) by Raja Ram Mohan Roy, the Samachar Chandrika, Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar (Persian newspapers), the Bombay Samachar and the Gujarat Newspaper were some of the other forms taken by print culture and print technology.

items.stem:
What were the effects of the spread of print culture for poor people in nineteenth century India ?
or
What was the impact of print culture on the poor people of India during the 19th century?
items.answer: The effects of the spread of print culture for poor people in nineteenth century India were: (1) large scale printing maintained reasonable prices for books, so the poor too enjoyed reading; (2) many of them got employment in printing presses and print shops; (3) the spread of print culture helped to restrict excessive drinking among the poor, to bring literacy, to give way to the shackles of the caste system and to propagate the message of nationalism; (4) they became aware of national, international and local news through cheap printed material; (5) with the Vernacular Press, nationalist ideas made a home in the minds of poor people; and (6) caste discrimination was brought up through print culture, which associated poor people with the nationalist freedom struggle.
